title: Google Boosts News and Link Visibility in AI Mode as Publisher Traffic Falls
excerpt: Google will place inline links higher in AI Overviews and AI Mode, expand news carousels worldwide, and grow its publisher licensing pilot past 400 outlets.
body:
• Google will show inline links higher up and more frequently in AI Overviews and AI Mode, and make end-of-answer links more prominent with image thumbnails.
  • Link carousels for timely news articles and Preferred Sources are expanding to more locations and languages.
  • Publishers have warned of steep traffic losses; Chartbeat data cited by Google coverage puts the drop at 40% for news sites between July 2025 and July 2026.
  • Google also said more than 400 publishers now take part in its News AI licensing pilot, with Axios, CNN and the Financial Times newly added.

Google announced on Thursday that it will display links to websites and news articles more prominently and higher up in its AI-powered search results, responding to warnings from publishers and brands about a sharp decline in traffic. The changes cover both AI Overviews, the summaries shown at the top of search, and AI Mode, the more conversational search experience Google launched in March 2025, according to The Economic Times reporting an AFP account of the announcement.

Google began adding AI to search more than two years ago, launching AI Overviews in May 2024. Instead of only listing links as traditional search did, the features generate a summarised answer, with links embedded in or placed around that answer.

What Is Changing

Inline links will now appear higher up in responses more frequently, Google said in its announcement covered by 9to5Google. Links at the end of some responses, in a section intended for digging deeper, will be redesigned to be more engaging, with image thumbnails and a more clickable design.

For timely stories, link carousels that sit below an AI Overview and show article headlines with images are expanding to additional locations and languages, after being announced in May. Preferred Sources, which lets users prioritise outlets they choose, is expanding on the same basis; Google said use of that customisation has grown sevenfold since launch.

Google is also testing two additions: a section at the very top of a response for the one or two official sites where a specific task can be completed or exact information found, with context on why each link is useful, and clickable publisher and creator names on video results that lead to their Search profiles.

Why Publishers Pushed Back

The redesign follows sustained evidence that AI summaries reduce clicks. Several studies have found users open suggested links far less often when an answer is already summarised for them. Chartbeat data cited in coverage of the announcement put news publishers' Google referral traffic down 40 percent between July 2025 and July 2026.

In France, the newspaper group Apig told the competition authority in August that AI summaries breached agreements reached with publishers in 2022, a sign the dispute is becoming regulatory as well as commercial. Google noted AI Overviews already reach more than two billion monthly users across more than 200 countries, a figure Alphabet chief executive Sundar Pichai cited at its second-quarter 2025 results, which makes the placement of a link inside those answers commercially decisive.

Licensing Alongside Links

Alongside the product changes, Google said its News AI licensing pilot now includes more than 400 publishers. The programme pays publishers for delivery and use of enhanced content to develop AI features, including in-depth article overviews on Google News publisher pages. Axios, CNN and the Financial Times are among the newly added partners, according to coverage of the announcement.

What This Means for Readers and Publishers

For readers, the practical change is simple: sources should be visible earlier in an AI answer, and the outlet behind a video or article should be one click away, rather than buried below a summary. For publishers, including Indian and diaspora news sites that depend on Google referrals, the test will be measured in traffic, not design. If higher, more clickable links do not restore click-through, pressure for licensing payments and regulatory intervention is likely to grow.

Google described the moves as continued, substantial increases to the presence of links in its AI experiences. The rollout of carousels and Preferred Sources to more languages will determine how quickly readers outside the United States see the difference.
